newsitem.title: USA: Helsinki summit offers Clinton a welcome diversion.
newsitem.headline: Helsinki summit offers Clinton a welcome diversion.

text.p: This week's Helsinki summit will give President Bill Clinton, who is beset by scandals at home, an opportunity to shift the spotlight from his stymied domestic agenda to the heady world of superpower diplomacy.

Meeting on Thursday and Friday in Finland, the site of past U.S.-Soviet encounters, Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin are expected to concentrate on the thorny matter of expanding the NATO security alliance into eastern Europe.

The summit, postponed by one day to give Clinton more time to recover from knee surgery after he fell in Florida last Friday, will also cover a wide range of other matters including arms control and Russian economic reform.

For Clinton, it may provide a welcome respite from the relentless media grilling about his Democratic Party's fund raising during the 1996 election campaign that returned him to the White House for a second four-year term.

The controversy embraces everything from allegations that the Chinese government may have sought to funnel money to U.S. politicians -- which China denies -- to Clinton's practice of inviting big donors to stay overnight at the White House.

It is the latest chapter in the president's up-and-down political career, and even his press secretary Mike McCurry concedes that Clinton is resigned to the media glare. "He's well aware of the fact we're in a feeding frenzy and you just have to endure it," McCurry told reporters recently.
The summit might have been expected to be a triumphant moment for Yeltsin and Clinton, both of whom won re-election last year. But neither has enjoyed a post-election honeymoon.
Yeltsin is reasserting his authority within Russia after a bout of pneumonia this year and quintuple-bypass surgery last year that kept him out of the political arena for months.

For his part, Clinton has spent much of the four months since his re-election answering questions about the growing campaign finance controversy. The Democratic Party has given back nearly $3 million in questionable donations while officials up to Vice President Al Gore have had to defend their fund-raising tactics.

As the fund-raising controversy has simmered on, Clinton has not been able to translate his election victory into any tangible result on balancing the budget with the Republicans who control both houses of Congress.

Even his budget director, Franklin Raines, admits there has been no movement on balancing the budget, which Clinton has said repeatedly is his top priority. "I talk to as many people as I can to see if we can make some progress," he told Reuters last week. "But as of now, we're not making any measurable progress."

For the first time since Clinton's re-election there have been signs of an erosion in his popularity, with two polls last week showing concern about the fund-raising controversy. An ABC poll found Clinton's approval rating had slipped to 55 percent from 60 percent in January, while a CBS poll put it at 56 percent, down from 63 percent two months ago.

Brookings Institution analyst Stephen Hess said summits sometimes boost poll ratings, but the bounce is usually brief and the growing frequency of such meetings -- Helsinki will be the 11th for Clinton and Yeltsin -- may diminish even that.
"They are very good, but very short-lived," Hess said. "You can see blips up, sometimes very considerable ones ... but after that it settles back very quickly."
